corrected_claim.text: Wiedrich's battery stood on a hill north of the Baltimore turnpike near the cemetery and east of the town (Hunt: in front of the cemetery entrance). During the afternoon it skirmished with a rebel battery posted near the York road. About 5 p.m., when the Union infantry that had advanced through the town was repulsed, Wiedrich changed the direction of his pieces, opened with shells on the columns advancing from the town, and then fired canister at the enemy that appeared in front; the fire was kept up until late in the evening. Howard and Hunt place the enemy's single attempt to turn the right at about 4.30 p.m. and say Wiedrich's battery broke the line. Nothing in the reports ties this fire to the railroad cut (the cut lies on Oak Ridge, far from his front).

corrected_claim.text: At 5.25 p.m. Hancock wrote from the cemetery: when he arrived 'an hour since' he found the troops had given up the front of Gettysburg and the town; the troops had taken a position in the cemetery that 'cannot well be taken' but is easily turned; Slocum was coming on the ground and taking position on the right; there were no troops on the left, the Third Corps not having reported; Gibbon had better march up to a commanding position on the right or left; the battle was quiet and he thought all would be right until night; trains had been sent back; 'I think we can retire; if not, we can fight here, as the ground appears not unfavorable with good troops'; he would soon transfer the command to Slocum. His later report puts his arrival at 3 p.m.; the 'an hour since' of the dispatch is carried as a conflict (arrival hour).

sub_claims.claim: Dispatch headed 5.25 (p.m. bracketed by the Official Records editors), Jul 1, addressed 'General:' (no addressee printed in the text read); Hancock's report calls it a communication to the major-general commanding, sent by Captain Parker of his staff
On arriving 'an hour since' he found our troops had given up the front of Gettysburg and the town; they had taken a position in the cemetery that cannot well be taken but is easily turned
The sentence 'we can fight here' is conditional: 'I think we can retire; if not, we can fight here, as the ground appears not unfavorable with good troops'
Arrival hour of Hancock: 3 p.m. (his report) against 'an hour since' at 5.25 (about 16:25) and 4 p.m. (Howard's dispatch)
sub_claims.note: conflict carried as scenarios; the recorded delegated default C-039 is the window about 15:00-16:00

corrected_claim.text: Slocum moved the corps to Two Taverns on the morning of Jul 1 and resumed the march when news came that the First and Eleventh Corps were engaged. Geary, at Two Taverns by 11 a.m., advanced at about 2 p.m., reported to Hancock, who sent him to the extreme left, and by 5 p.m. had two regiments of his First Brigade on the hills south and west of the town, the rest along the line to the Baltimore turnpike and the Second Brigade with two guns in reserve about 2 miles out; the division rested on its arms during the night. Williams' division was directed by a cross-road toward the Hanover road to take an eminence about a mile east of the town, found it held by the enemy and, when about to assault, was called back as the Union forces had retired behind the town; it bivouacked nearer the Baltimore pike. corrected_claim.event: Williams' 1st Division marches to Two Taverns, where it hears that the First and Eleventh Corps are engaged, moves up the pike, turns by a cross-road toward the Hanover road to take an eminence about a mile east of the town, finds it held by the enemy, is ordered to withdraw when about to assault because the Union forces have retired behind the town, and takes a position nearer the Baltimore pike (about sunset, three-quarters of a mile to the rear), where it bivouacs; Ruger commands the division and Williams the corps
corrected_claim.unit: 1st Division, XII Corps (Brig. Gen. Williams; Brig. Gen. Ruger from the evening), Brig. Gen. Williams commanding the corps
corrected_claim.place: Two Taverns; cross-road to the Hanover road about a mile east of Gettysburg; position near the Baltimore pike

time_window.text: Jul 1, afternoon to night (Ruger: about sunset the division moved to the rear and stayed the night)
time_window.basis: Williams OR27-1-R272 pp.771 and 773; Ruger OR27-1-R273 p.777. Window limits: the afternoon of Jul 1 to the night of Jul 1-2; no hours are printed except 'about sunset'. A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: The seed's order of events is corrected: at Two Taverns Williams learned that the First and Eleventh Corps were engaged (not yet that they had retired); the division then moved up the pike and turned by a cross-road toward the Hanover road to seize a commanding hill east of the town; the hill was found held by the enemy and, when the division was about to assault, it was ordered to withdraw because the Union forces had retired behind the town. It then took a position nearer the Baltimore pike and bivouacked; Ruger puts the move to a position three-quarters of a mile to the rear 'about sunset'. Slocum turned the temporary command of the corps over to Williams and Ruger took the division. The reports do not name Culp's Hill for the hill east of the town.
corrected_claim.marking: tier glyph on every sub-claim that is not documented

sub_claims.claim: At Two Taverns the division received information of the engagement of the First and Eleventh Corps with the enemy beyond Gettysburg
It moved rapidly up the pike and near Rock Creek was directed by a cross-road toward the Hanover road to occupy an eminence a mile or so east of Gettysburg, which was found in possession of the enemy

When about to assault the position the division was ordered to withdraw, as the Union forces had retired behind the town (information of the retreat was received at this point, not before the march to the hill)

To preserve communications it took a position nearer the Baltimore pike and bivouacked for the night; Ruger: about sunset it moved to a position about three-quarters of a mile in rear and so remained during the night of the 1st

Slocum turned the temporary command of the corps to Williams; Ruger took the division (the same day or at daylight on Jul 2: Ruger writes that he took command of the division after the daylight picket shots of Jul 2)
sub_claims.note: hour of the change of command differs between Williams (Jul 1) and Ruger (Jul 2 daylight)

corrected_claim.text: Grover (7th Indiana) reports that on the afternoon of Jul 1, by Wadsworth's order, the regiment took position on the hill east of Gettysburg, then the extreme right of the Union line, and began a temporary breastwork; during the following night a force of the enemy attempted to penetrate the line but was easily driven off, supposing itself confronted by a heavy force; on the night of the 1st Sergeant Hussey, unassisted, captured a lieutenant of the 25th Virginia and drove off a squad of 20 men. Ewell reports that Johnson, after forming his line on this side of the wooded hill, sent a reconnoitering party to it; near the summit it was met by a superior force that captured part of it while the rest escaped; Johnson therefore refrained from taking the hill and, at daybreak, it was too late for a change. The tie between the two accounts is an inference; the seed's 'and man' (a second prisoner) is not in Grover's report.
corrected_claim.marking: tier glyph on every sub-claim that is not documented; the link between the 7th Indiana's capture and Johnson's party is shown as inferred

sub_claims.claim: By Wadsworth's command the 7th Indiana took up a position on the hill east of Gettysburg on the afternoon of Jul 1, then the extreme right of the line, and immediately began a temporary breastwork
During the night a force of the enemy attempted to penetrate the line and was easily driven off
On the night of the 1st Sergeant (William) Hussey, Company B, unassisted, captured a lieutenant of the 25th Virginia and drove off a squad of 20 men

Johnson, after forming his line this side of the wooded hill, sent a reconnoitering party to report the enemy's position; near the summit it was met by a superior force which captured a portion of it, the rest escaping
Johnson would refrain from attacking the hill until Ewell had notice that the enemy held it; day was breaking and it was too late for a change
The Union capture (7th Indiana) and the Confederate loss of part of a reconnoitering party are the same incident
sub_claims.note: inference: the lieutenant belongs to the 25th Virginia of Johnson's division (Higginbotham p.536 sends its skirmishers out at twilight of Jul 1); no report names both sides

sub_claims.claim: The Union captured an officer and one man (the seed wording)
sub_claims.note: Grover names a lieutenant captured and a squad of 20 driven off; no second prisoner is named

corrected_claim.text: Hancock says Wadsworth's division and a battery were placed on the eminence just across the turnpike, which the division held to the end of the operations, and that he sent Geary's division to the high ground near Round Top. Doubleday records that Hancock directed him to send a force to support a battery on a lower range of hills about 100 yards east of the cemetery position and that he sent the rest of Wadsworth's division there, after which orders from Howard, who ranked Hancock, to send the troops in another direction caused some delay and confusion. Howard says Hancock was to arrange the troops and place the batteries on the left of the Baltimore pike while he took the right, and that Wadsworth's division was sent to a height to the right and rear. Wadsworth: on the evening of the 1st he was ordered to occupy a hill on the right of the cemetery. Hancock's exact words to Wadsworth are not in any report. The seed's 'Little Round Top' is Hancock's 'Round Top Mountain' (Geary, T1-176).

corrected_claim.text: The reports give the 123rd New York's breastwork on Jul 2: after being moved toward the town, 'into the woods to the right of Cemetery Hill', the regiment, in the front line of the brigade, built a strong breastwork along its front; McDougall puts the arrival there after about 11 a.m. and says the rear line stood behind a stone wall with the front line parallel and about 40 paces in advance. The seed's date (Jul 1 evening, from a soldier's letter), the distance 'about 10 rods (165 ft) in front of a heavy stone wall' and the pre-existing wall are carried as a lead: the reports say about 40 paces (about 100 feet at 30 inches to the pace) and give Jul 2. corrected_claim.text: Coulter's report of the First Brigade: the brigade, transferred to him about 5 p.m. on Jul 1 when the division was formed in the cemetery, retired through the town and was re-formed about 5 p.m.; later in the evening it moved toward the left, took position on the left of the Eleventh Corps and, having built breastworks of such materials as were at hand, remained there in support of the batteries until relieved by the Third Division, Second Corps, about noon the next day. 'About 7 o'clock in the evening' the brigade moved farther left to support the Third Corps under a considerable artillery fire, and 'about 10 p.m.' was placed on the Emmitsburg and Gettysburg road, from which it was relieved at daylight on the 3d: these two hours are Jul 2 (the Third Corps fought on Jul 2; the brigade is relieved on the 3d). The seed's 'moves left to support III Corps about 19:00' on Jul 1 is not supported. Other units of the division report the same evening works: the 107th Pennsylvania (threw up strong breastworks on the left of Cemetery Hill that night) and the 11th Pennsylvania (took position in rear of breastworks on the south side of the town), Baxter's brigade (temporary breastworks near the Emmitsburg road at about 5 p.m.).

corrected_claim.text: Johnson, marching from Scotland by the Cashtown road, did not arrive in time to take part in the fighting. Nicholls' brigade, in front, was at about 7 o'clock on the Cashtown road marching toward Gettysburg when Johnson ordered it east along the railroad about three-quarters of a mile from the town. Jones's brigade left camp at 7 a.m., reached the town 'late in the afternoon', passed the depot to the left of the town and formed line about dark; Richardson (42nd Virginia) puts the arrival 'about sunset'; Steuart's brigade came 'toward evening' and, marching through part of the town and along the York railroad, formed line to the northeast; Walker's brigade arrived on the evening and took position after nightfall on the southeast side of the town near the Hanover road, on Culp's farm. Johnson himself: 'late on the night of July 1' he formed line of battle in a ravine in an open field, Nicholls on the right next Jones, Steuart and Walker on the left, pickets well to the front, the troops sleeping on their arms. Lee: Johnson 'did not reach Gettysburg until a late hour'. All of these are carried as the arrival window; no single hour is picked.

corrected_claim.text: Lee wrote that Ewell was instructed to carry the hill occupied by the enemy if he found it practicable, but to avoid a general engagement until the other divisions arrived; Ewell decided to await Johnson's division, which reached Gettysburg at a late hour, and the enemy meanwhile occupied the point Ewell meant to seize. Ewell wrote that on entering the town he received a message from the commanding general to attack the hill if he could do so to advantage; he could not bring artillery to bear, all the troops with him were jaded by twelve hours' marching and fighting, Cemetery Hill was not assailable from the town, and he determined to take a wooded hill to his left with Johnson's division. Early's report: he rode to urge an immediate advance, sent word to Hill that if he would send a division the hill could be taken, learned that Johnson was coming and that it was determined to occupy a wooded hill to the left of Cemetery Hill, but the division arrived late and 'no effort ... was made that night'. In 1877 Early added the reasons he knew: Rodes' division had lost about 2,500, only two of his own brigades were available, and constant reports of an enemy advance on the York road. The seed's 'narrow streets' and 'lack of support from Hill' do not appear in the reports; Early's 1877 paper has Hill's troops not advanced beyond Seminary Ridge. The seed's 'Early opposes' is corrected in T1-187. Rodes' own report (p.555) adds that the corps commander had told him in the midst of the engagement that the general commanding did not wish a general engagement brought on, that the enemy was forming a formidable line on the heights back of the town, and that to attack it with his division alone, diminished by a loss of 2,500 men (the page image prints 2,500; the archive.org OCR text reads 3,600), 'would have been absurd'; Early's 1877 figure for the same loss is about 2,500.

corrected_claim.text: The National Park Service writes that the Mary Thompson House, built in the 1840s, served as Lee's headquarters and that on the morning of July 1, 1863 Lee rode just north of Gettysburg and established his headquarters in the farmstead residence of Mary Thompson. That differs from the seed's 'evening'; no Official Records passage names the Thompson house or gives Lee's place on the evening of Jul 1. The only place the sources name for Lee on the evening of Jul 1 is Early's account of a conference with Ewell and Rodes on the back porch of a small house north of the town near the Carlisle road. Longstreet (1896) reports to 'General Lee's head-quarters' at daylight on Jul 2 without naming a place. An illustration by Benson Lossing titled 'Confederate Headquarters' (a scene of September 1866, published in 1877) shows the repaired house (caption in the NPS landscape report); the same report says the house became famous for its association with Confederate headquarters following the Union retreat from Seminary Ridge on July 1, with the headquarters operations probably extending into the surrounding area, notably the Dustman orchard across the turnpike. The year of building (1833 Stone Sentinels; 1840s NPS), the 'Thaddeus Stevens building' reading of Wikipedia and the burning of Mary Thompson's fences for firewood have no passage in the local texts and stay unsupported. The seed calls Lee-in-the-cupola a rumour. Jacobs (1864, p.41) writes, in his account of Jul 3 before the 2.30 p.m. cannonade, that 'during the day General Lee had reconnoitred our position from the College cupola'; that is the statement of one resident, with no source given, for Jul 3 and not for the evening of Jul 1, and no cupola scene is shown for Jul 1. Added by the second reading: a relief worker's letter of the consecration day (Nov 1863) says the party 'saw Lee's headquarters' on Seminary Hill; Hoke (1887) places Lee's headquarters in a stone house a short distance out on the Chambersburg Pike and says Lee took observations from the cupola of Pennsylvania College (a later book; no day, no hour, no house named).

corrected_claim.text: The National Park Service landscape report says: troops began to arrive on Cemetery Hill on July 1 when Howard posted a reserve of his Eleventh Corps; late in the day, as Union troops retreated, they reinforced the defensive lines around Cemetery Hill; lines of artillery were positioned near the summit along the northern and western borders of Evergreen Cemetery with caissons and horses among the grave plots; it was reported that General Howard ordered troops to lay the headstones flat on the ground to prevent their destruction; troops tore down wood and stone fences and rebuilt stone fences as breastworks. Battle damage included bullet holes and cracks in some grave markers, damage to grave-plot fences, removal of planks from the fences along the Baltimore pike, and a damaged gatehouse. The report does not date the laying flat of the headstones or the fence damage within the three days, says nothing of 'iron fences', and names no monument destroyed. The seed's attribution of the night of Jul 1 is therefore not documented; the damage is shown as occurring during the battle, with the evening of Jul 1 as the earliest time. Added by the second reading: newspapers of July 1863 say that in the cannonade of Jul 3 the tombstones were knocked over and iron railings torn (Boston Journal's correspondent, printed Jul 23), that tombstones and beautiful monuments were demolished (Bellows Falls Times, Jul 10), and that monuments and headstones lay overturned and graves were trampled by horses (Chicago Daily Tribune, Jul 12); none dates this damage to the evening of Jul 1.

corrected_claim.text: On Jul 1 Greene's brigade was posted on the left with the division, about half a mile to the right of Sugar Loaf Mountain in front of the Taneytown road, with 'no incidents to note'; the division rested on its arms during the night. On Jul 2 Geary was relieved by the Third Corps and at 5 a.m. placed his division on the right of the centre of the line; Greene took position at about 6 a.m. on the crest of the hill and 'as soon as we were in position, we began to intrench ourselves and throw up breastworks'. Godard (60th New York): at or about 6 a.m. the regiment assumed position and threw up intrenchments by Greene's order, working until about 9 a.m. when they were completed; Ireland (137th): the breastworks were completed about noon; Hammerstein (78th): a breastwork of trees and dirt was soon thrown up; Stegman (102nd): the men were ordered to build breastworks of cord-wood and rock. Greene's report prints 'By 12 o'clock we had a good cover for the men': the OCR text reads '13 o'clock', and the printed number was read on the page image (printed page 856, PDF page 880 of the part-1 scan) as 12. The seed's 'construction began the night of Jul 1-2' (New York state agency page) is contradicted by Greene's and Geary's own accounts; the 'done about noon' (Gettysburg Daily) agrees with Ireland for one regiment.

Dawn: McAllister (11th New Jersey, Carr's brigade) wrote 'morning dawned [with] considerable fog'; Haskell, of the Second Corps staff, wrote that before six the corps was up to the field and that 'the morning was thick and sultry, the sky overcast with low, vapory clouds' and the men 'looked like giants there in the mist'; Jacobs (resident, 1864): 'the morning was pleasant, the air was calm, the sun shone mildly through a smoky atmosphere'. corrected_claim.text: Butterfield's order of 1.10 p.m.: Hancock to turn over the Second Corps to Gibbon, go to the front and, if Reynolds is dead, 'assume command of the corps there assembled, viz, the Eleventh, First, and Third, at Emmitsburg', advising Meade whether the ground is a better one to fight on. Hancock: at 3 p.m. he arrived at Gettysburg and assumed command; Wadsworth's division and a battery were placed on the eminence across the turnpike. Howard (dispatch): Hancock arrived at 4 p.m. Hunt (BL-3, 1888): Wadsworth led the 7th Indiana to Culp's Hill; Hancock, received at the hill, ordered Wadsworth at once to Culp's Hill to secure the position. Doubleday: Hancock directed him to send a force to support a battery on a lower range of hills some 100 yards east; he sent the rest of Wadsworth's division, then Howard's counter-orders caused delay. Smith: his brigade, formed in mass in rear of the hill, advanced through the cemetery to the front of the hill overlooking the town; its arrival 'in good order and with full ranks' contributed to holding the hill. The seed's 'about 1,600 fresh' and 'tells Doubleday to send every man' are not in these reports; the arrival hours 15:00, before 16:00, 16:00 and 16:30 are carried as scenarios under the recorded default C-039 (about 15:00-16:00).

corrected_claim.text: Documented: the Eleventh Corps hospital occupied the house and farm of Geo. Spangler, its divisions consolidated under Dr. Armstrong; the Sanitary Commission's associate secretary (report signed Washington, Aug. 15, 1863) puts it at 1,900 wounded, 100 of whom were said to be Confederates, in a table (Eleventh Corps 1,800 Union and 100 Confederate) that he calls 'approximative only' and that does not date its counts. The National Park Service says the farm complex 'additionally served as the 11th Corps field hospital' and that this hospital was the site of Armistead's death; its 1932 list places the hospital tablet 700 feet east of the house. Not in any text read: the hour at which the staff took the farm, the first wounded, the operations through the night, the counts of 2,000, 1,500 and 1,000, and the date of the Sanitary Commission's count. The only George Spangler farm in the Official Records is the bivouac farm near Emmitsburg (R060 p.326), unrelated. The counts are carried as the recorded delegated default C-038 (range 1,000 to 2,000, all five values listed, no headline number), unchanged here; two of the five values, 1,800 and 1,900, now have a source.
